newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Croatia's Tudjman symbolises Balkan old guard.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman symbolises Balkan old guard.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman will be sworn in on Tuesday for a second five-year term in an occasion that will highlight how little has changed in the top echelons of Balkan politics.
More than six years after the federation of Yugoslavia fragmented and plunged into war, the same men still hold power in every one of the six former constituent republics.
Each has been re-elected in democratic votes, despite being responsible for the nationalist policies which led to a war which killed 200,000 and left millions destitute.
Diplomats in the region say there are several reasons why so little has changed and add that it will be hard to make real progress until a new batch of leaders comes to power.
"It's proving difficult to move forward...We have made progress but we might have made more in different circumstances and with a different set of people," a Western diplomat said.
Political opposition in former Yugoslavia remains weak -- a legacy of 50 years of communism and the result of loyalty to strong leaders who brought independence to the republics.

"It's almost unprecedented for a region which has seen such turmoil over a long period of time that you have the same indidividuals still in power, it's an interesting phenomenon," another Western diplomat in the region said.
"Since 1990 these people have held firmly to power in the tradition they came from, which is communist, bureaucratic, centralised," said a United Nations official.
Slovenia, under the leadership of Milan Kucan, 56, was first to secede from the federation. Kucan was elected president in 1992 and is expected to win fresh elections later this year.

Next to go was Croatia, under Franjo Tudjman. He won a resounding victory in a new presidential election in June and the 76-year-old leader now has five more years to fulfil Croatian hopes of joining the Western European family of nations.

In Bosnia, a three-man collective presidency is headed by Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem, who led the country to independence in 1992, precipitating a 43-month war. He was the Bosnian republic's leader in the Yugoslav federation.

Slobodan Milosevic successfully engineered a takeover of the post-war Yugoslav federation presidency in July from his position as president of Serbia in a manoeuvre to remain political supremo in Belgrade and power-broker in the region of old Yugoslavia.
The post of president of the federation linking Serbia and Montenegro had hitherto been mainly ceremonial.
Momir Bulatovic, 40, became president of Montenegro in 1993 and is running for re-election now. He was the republic's president in the former federation.
In Macedonia, the last of the six former republics, Kiro Gligorov, 80, was re-elected in October 1994 after becoming the first president of independent Macedonia in 1991.

What confounds Western observers is that, much as they would like to see some, if not all, of these leaders out of office, each has won a mandate in post-communist elections. There is little the West can do and even the political opposition remains weak and directionless in many of the countries.
Sporadic local election victories have failed to translate into victories at national level and nationalist leaders are still well ensconced in power.
In Croatia, the opposition is divided between several parties who are reluctant to form coalitions and are hampered by limited access to the state-controlled media.

The spirit seen during three months of street protests in the Serbian capital of Belgrade when Milosevic, 55, annulled opposition victories in municipal elections, has dimmed as the coalition collapsed amid bickering over power-sharing.
In Bosnia, four opposition parties have teamed up with Izetbegovic's Moslem party for local elections next month..
Izetbegovic is the only leader in the region who has said he will not stand for president again.
"A general fear of the population is to change horses. Look at the alternatives -- there are none, no one who can unite the people," one Western diplomat said.
Another diplomat admitted the West's hands were tied.
"We are faced with a dilemma -- how much can we interfere? We can't force people to vote for leaders that we would find more useful in managing the problems of the Balkans."
But with an average age of 63, the former Yugoslavia's leaders cannot go on for ever.
"We are waiting for nature to take it's course -- to solve the problems that politicians haven't been able to," a diplomat said.
